scenes.say: Sort a million ages. A comparison sort needs twenty million steps. Counting needs one million. By the end, you'll explain why s t d colon colon sort is fast, and when it's the wrong tool.

lines.cue: s t d colon colon sort

scenes.say: Today's plan. Insertion and merge sort first. Then quicksort, and what s t d colon colon sort really does. Finally, counting sort for small ranges.
lines: Sort a million ages in linear time

scenes.title: Sort the array
scenes.statement: Rearrange numbers into increasing order, and say what that costs.
scenes.say: Put numbers in increasing order, and say what that costs. Start with five, two, four, six, one, three. We get one through six. First, the simplest method.

scenes.head: Sorting a hand of cards
scenes.say: You already know insertion sort from card games. Hold sorted cards in your left hand. Pick up the next card, called the key. Slide it left past every bigger card, then drop it in the gap.

scenes.head: Insertion sort on 5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3
scenes.say: Take this array of six cards. Pick up the two. Five is bigger, so it slides right. Drop the two in the gap. Next, four. Five slides right, and four lands beside two. Six is already in place. Now one. Everything slides right, and one lands at the front. Last, three. Six, five, four slide, and three drops in.

scenes.head: Insertion sort in code
scenes.say: In code, the key is a of i. While the cell on its left is bigger, copy it one step right. Then drop the key in the gap. Worst case, a reversed array: every key slides past everything before it, about n squared over two moves. Already sorted? Nothing slides. O of n means work grows in step with n.
Your turn. The array is already sorted, one through six. How much work does insertion sort do? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Insertion sort on an already sorted array?

scenes.head: Slides to sort six cards
scenes.say: Slides to sort six cards. Sorted input means no slides, so O of n. Six sorted cards: zero slides. Our shuffled six: nine. Reversed: fifteen.
That's why insertion sort wins on tiny or nearly sorted arrays. That answers the sort-the-array problem.
lines: Tiny or nearly sorted? Insertion wins.

scenes.title: Sort faster than O(n²)
scenes.statement: Insertion sort needs half a trillion moves for a million reversed items. Can we do better?
scenes.say: Insertion sort chokes on big input. A million items in reverse order? Half a trillion moves. We want about twenty million steps instead, and merge sort gets there.

scenes.head: Divide and conquer
scenes.say: Merge sort uses divide and conquer. Split the pile in half. Sort each half the same way. Then merge two sorted piles by comparing their top cards.

scenes.head: Merge sort, step 1: split
scenes.say: Take this six card array. Cut it in half. Cut each half again. Keep cutting. A single card is already sorted, so cutting stops there. Six cards need three cuts: log base two of six, rounded up. Work happens on the way back up.

scenes.head: Merge sort, step 2: merge
scenes.say: Now merge back up. To merge two sorted piles, compare the fronts and take the smaller. Five and two: two goes first. Six and one: one goes first. Merge the pair two and five with four: two, four, five. Merge one and six with three: one, three, six. Last merge: one through six. Every level touches all six cards. Three levels: O of n log n.

scenes.head: Merge sort: split and recurse
scenes.say: In code: sort the left half, sort the right half, then merge them. A range of one card or none is already sorted, so the recursion stops there. The middle splits the range.

scenes.head: The merge, and why it is stable
scenes.say: Merge walks both halves with i and j, always taking the smaller front into a temp vector. Notice the less or equal sign. On a tie, the left card wins, so equal cards keep their order. That's called stable. The price: O of n extra memory.
Your turn. One thousand twenty four cards. How many times can you halve the pile before every card stands alone? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Halvings from 1,024 cards to single cards?

scenes.head: Why merge sort is O(n log n)
scenes.say: Ten. Two to the tenth is one thousand twenty four. Each of the ten levels merges all one thousand twenty four cards, so about ten thousand steps. That's n log n: log n levels, n work each.

scenes.head: Say these out loud
scenes.say: Three things to say out loud. Stable means equal items keep their input order. Merge sort is stable if you merge with less or equal, not less than. Insertion sort? Great for tiny or nearly sorted arrays. That answers the faster-sort problem.

scenes.title: Sort in place, no merging
scenes.statement: Sort an array without extra memory, by fixing one element's final spot at a time.

example.output: 3 lands at index 2: smaller left, bigger right

scenes.say: Can we sort without any extra memory, fixing one element's final spot at a time? Take five, two, four, six, one, three, with the boss, the pivot, three. Three lands at index two, smaller cards left, bigger right.

scenes.head: Lining up a crowd by height
scenes.say: Quicksort lines up a crowd by height. Pick one person as the boss, the pivot. Everyone shorter goes left. Everyone taller goes right. Now the boss stands in the final spot and never moves again. Repeat on each side.

scenes.head: Partition around the last card
scenes.say: Take this six card array. The pivot is the last card: three. Pointer i marks where the next small card goes. Pointer j scans. Five: bigger, skip. Two: smaller, swap it left. Four: bigger. Six: bigger. One: smaller, swap it left too. Last, swap the pivot into slot i. Three is home.

items.label: pivot
items.cue: The pivot is the last card

scenes.head: Partition in code
scenes.say: In code, the pivot is the last card. Scan j from the left. When a card is smaller than the pivot, swap it to slot i and move i forward. At the end, swap the pivot into slot i, and return where it landed.

scenes.head: Then recurse on both sides
scenes.say: Three is placed. Now do the same on each side. Left side, two and one, becomes one, two. Right side: six, five, four. Pivot four lands in its place, and five, six fall into line. No merging needed, because every pivot is already home.

scenes.head: Quicksort in code
scenes.say: The recursion: partition, then sort what's left of the pivot, and what's right of it. Stop when a range has fewer than two cards. On our array, it prints one through six.
Your turn. The array is already sorted, and the pivot is the last card. How many cards land left of the pivot? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Sorted 1 to 6, pivot is the last card. Left side?

scenes.head: The worst case: a sorted array
scenes.say: Five. Every card is smaller than six, so all five land on the left, and the right side is empty. Next round faces five cards, then four, then three. That's n rounds of n work, about n squared over two comparisons: O of n squared. Random pivots avoid it. That answers the in-place problem.

scenes.title: What does std::sort do?
scenes.statement: Say what std::sort really does, and how to give it your own order.

example.input: words by length: banana, fig, apple, kiwi

scenes.say: What does s t d colon colon sort do? Can you set your own order? Say, words by length: fig, kiwi, apple, banana. It's an introsort: a mix of three sorts. A comparator says which item comes first.

scenes.head: Introsort: three sorts in one
scenes.say: Call s t d colon colon sort. In common implementations, it's an introsort: quicksort first. If recursion gets too deep, it switches to heap sort, so the worst case stays O of n log n. On tiny ranges, it uses insertion sort.

scenes.head: A comparator: shorter words first
scenes.say: For a custom order, pass a comparator: does x come before y? Here, shorter words first. It must say strictly less. Fig, kiwi, apple, banana.
Your turn. Bob and Cat both scored ninety, and Bob came first in the input. Which call guarantees Bob stays ahead? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Equal scores, bob before cat. Which call keeps that?

scenes.head: stable_sort keeps ties in order
scenes.say: Stable sort, with greater than. Plain sort makes no promise about ties. Stable sort keeps equal items in input order, so Bob stays ahead of Cat. Amy, with eighty five, comes last.

scenes.head: Traps and trade-offs
scenes.say: The traps. Is sort stable? No. Use stable sort. A comparator with greater or equal is undefined behavior, so stay strict. Quicksort versus merge? Quick is in place, merge is stable but needs memory. Worst case of s t d sort? Still n log n. That answers the problem.

chapters.title: Beat n log n with counting

scenes.title: Sort a million ages
scenes.statement: Sort values that are small whole numbers, like ages 0 to 120, faster than comparing.
scenes.say: Ages run from zero to one hundred twenty, so why compare at all? Take three, one, zero, three, four, one, three. Out comes zero, one, one, three, three, three, four.

scenes.head: Tally marks, not comparisons
scenes.say: Say you have ages, zero to one hundred twenty. Keep one tally per age. Then read the tallies in order. That's counting sort. No comparing, so the cost is n plus k, not n log n.

scenes.head: Counting sort: values 0 to 4
scenes.say: Say the ages are zero to four. Make one counter per value. Walk the input. Three bumps counter three. One bumps counter one. Zero bumps counter zero. Another three. Then four. Then another one. Then a last three. Now write each value out as often as its counter says: zero, one one, three three three, four.

scenes.head: Counting sort in code
scenes.say: In code: a counter array of size five, all zero. One pass counts. Then for each value, print it as many times as its counter says. Sorted. The cost is O of n plus k, where k is the value range. For a million ages, k is just one hundred twenty one.
Your turn. Which input should you sort by counting, not by comparing? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Which input should you sort by counting?

scenes.head: Counters you would need
scenes.say: Counters each method needs. Ages: one hundred twenty one counters, nothing. Ints up to a billion need a billion counters, about four gigabytes.
Names and doubles? Use plain sort. That answers the million-ages problem.

scenes.head: Insertion and merge, 20 seconds
scenes.say: Insertion sort? Slide each card into place, quadratic, or linear if already sorted. Merge sort? Split, sort the halves, merge. Why n log n? Log n levels of halving, and each level merges n items.
rows: slide each card into place: O(n²)
log n levels, each merges n items

scenes.head: The follow-ups
scenes.say: Stable? Equal items keep their order. When insertion sort? Tiny or nearly sorted arrays, where it's O of n. Common mistake? Less than instead of less or equal breaks stability: equal items can swap.
rows: breaks stability: equal items can swap

scenes.say: Quick self test. A million integers, each up to a billion. Counting sort, std sort, or insertion sort? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: Quicksort, 20 seconds
scenes.say: Quicksort? Pick a pivot, partition smaller left and bigger right, recurse. Worst case? O of n squared with bad pivots, like a sorted array. Quick or merge? Quick is in place, merge is stable. Counting or sort? A billion counters is about four GB, so sort wins.
rows: O(n²), bad pivots: avg is O(n log n)

scenes.head: What std::sort does
scenes.say: What does s t d sort do? Introsort: n log n worst case, not stable. When a comparator? Custom order, like shorter first.
rows: introsort: O(n log n), not stable
custom order, e.g. shorter first; strict `<`

scenes.head: Counting sort
scenes.say: Strict less, never less or equal. Counting sort? A small integer range k, in O of n plus k.
rows: small integer range k: O(n + k)

scenes.head: Practice before your interview
scenes.say: Solve these next. LeetCode seventy five, Sort Colors, is counting sort in disguise. LeetCode fifty six, Merge Intervals, sorts with a comparator first. LeetCode one forty eight, Sort List, is merge sort on a linked list.
rows: sort by start with a comparator
merge sort on a linked list

scenes.say: So say this. Insertion sort is quadratic, merge sort is n log n and stable. Quicksort partitions, and s t d sort is introsort. For a small integer range, counting sort is linear.
lines: Insertion O(n²); merge O(n log n), stable.
Small integer range: counting sort, O(n + k).
